I'm Jagdish, and I've been sleeping on my sister Preeti's sofa in Nagpur during my exams, so I hear a lot.
Every few evenings Preeti brings up money. Last night she had the electricity bill and the EMI letter in her hand. "Ashwin, we need to decide what we cut back on." Ashwin, honestly the funniest person I know, said, "Easy. We cut back on Jagdish." I laughed. So did he. Preeti smiled a small smile and said, "I mean it."
He did a whole routine about living on air and sunlight. Then he asked what was for dinner.
I don't know exactly what Preeti felt. But she folded the letter into a tiny square and didn't say much after. This morning she was doing sums on the back of an envelope, alone at six, while he slept.
Tonight she asked me to go for a walk so she could talk to Ashwin properly.

Yusuf, you asked how George and I stayed married forty years. Let old Elizabeth tell you about our worst year. We were twenty-five, I a nervous young wife, in a rented room in Kochi, and the milk bills were piling up. Every time I tried to talk about money, George made a joke. "Money is a myth invented by milkmen." Very funny. I laughed, every time, and every time I felt a little smaller, as if my worry were childish.

One night I laid all the bills in a line on the floor and said, "George, I am not laughing tonight. I'm frightened, and I feel alone with this." He started a joke, looked at my face, and stopped. Then he sat down on the floor with me. We went through every bill until two in the morning.

He never lost his humour. He just learned when to put it down.

qa.a: They lived in a rented room in Kochi.

qa.q: How did young Elizabeth feel each time George joked about money?
qa.a: Young Elizabeth felt dismissed and smaller each time, as if her worry were childish.

qa.a: Elizabeth laid out the bills and said plainly she was frightened and alone, and George stopped mid-joke and sat down to go through them.
